source.title: UXBench: Benchmarking User Experience in AI Assistants
source.authors: Mengze Hong; Xia Zeng; Zeyang Lei; Sheng Wang; Chen Jason Zhang; Di Jiang; Taiming Fu; Jinfeng Huang; Mengqiao Liu; Qinghe Chang; Haosheng Zou; Qiongyi Zhou; Sijun He;  Simonjmdeng; Minlong Peng; Di Liang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some extracted figure/table material is garbled, but the relevant scaling-trend results are described in text.
record.tranche_reason: Applies a model-evolution analysis to user-experience performance, a new evaluation setting, and reports a result on the trend.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test power-law loss in parameter count, tokens, or compute; extrapolation from small runs; compute-optimal allocation; or architecture sensitivity. Its relevant result is a correlation between model release time and UX response-generation scores. Other reported benchmark, judge, prompting, and recovery results do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: The only 'scaling' result correlates model release date with UX Eval Good% across closed frontier models. Parameter count, tokens, compute and pretraining loss are never measured or stated. Release time is a different construct from scale or loss, so no version, including V6, is tested. The paper uses 'scaling trend' and 'user-centric scaling laws' loosely, as discussion.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors call the trend positive but moderate or weak, even 'confirming a positive scaling trend'. They conclude that capability progress alone does not guarantee robust UX, and call for user-centric scaling laws. Their 'scaling' means model evolution over release time, not parameter, data or compute scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Uses release-time correlations and benchmark response-quality scores, not held-out pretraining-loss scaling fits, run-size sweeps, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported correlation weakens when lightweight flash/lite variants are excluded (ρ = 0.48, p = 0.082).

fits_no_version.finding: Across 16 frontier models, release date correlates moderately with UX Eval Good% (rho 0.52, p 0.043, wide CI). Excluding flash/lite variants weakens it to rho 0.48, p 0.082.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Newer model generations (by release date, not measured scale) improve user-perceived response quality only weakly.

record.problems: The trend analysis uses release time rather than directly measured model size, training tokens, compute, or pretraining loss. The reported correlation is moderate with a wide confidence interval, and becomes weaker and non-significant after excluding lightweight variants.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on a claim version were left out. Other model scores concern UX judging, response generation, recovery, prompts, or evaluator bias without testing the specified scaling relationships.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed size.
No other modality or training regime scaling.
No downstream performance against measured scale or pretraining loss. Model sizes and compute are not reported for any evaluated model.
No scaling-law fits or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 test and limits_scope label are not justified. Release time is a proxy unrelated to the versions' scale or loss variables. Table 10 (Qwen3-8B vs Qwen2.5-7B) is also a generational comparison at similar size, not a scaling test.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run losses from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture variation at fixed parameter count and its effect on loss.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study uses release time as a model-evolution proxy; it does not measure parameter count, training tokens, compute, or pretraining loss, nor directly test prediction from those quantities.
Dependence of scaling-law fits or compute-optimal splits on fitting and setup choices.

rows.subject: 16 models
rows.operation_detail: Correlated model release time with UX Eval response-generation quality.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between release time and UX quality
rows.note: The authors describe the trend as positive but weak/moderate. This is a release-time association, not a measured power law in model size, compute, tokens, or pretraining loss.
rows.check: Measures a Spearman correlation of release date with Good% (rho 0.52, CI 0.02–0.85), not performance against scale or pretraining loss. It cannot show V6's effect. The subject is 16 models plotted in Fig. 3, out of 26 evaluated.

rows.subject: 16 models, excluding lightweight flash/lite variants
rows.operation_detail: Recomputed the release-time/UX-quality correlation after excluding lightweight flash/lite variants.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between release time and UX quality
rows.note: The relationship is weaker and not statistically significant at conventional levels in this restricted analysis.
rows.check: The same release-date proxy with lightweight variants excluded (rho 0.48, p 0.082). It does not measure scale or loss.

rows.subject: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rows.operation_detail: Compared UX Eval response-generation quality with an earlier model in the same family.
rows.note: An example of within-family improvement; it does not establish a power-law relationship.
rows.check: A single within-family generational comparison (Gemini 3.1 Pro vs 2.5 Pro, +6.3pp; Table 3 shows 57.1% vs 50.8%). The model sizes are unknown, so this is not a scale comparison. It is also an illustrative example rather than a test.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Model release time versus UX Eval performance across the reported models
reader_labels.reason: The association is positive but described as weak/moderate, has a wide 95% confidence interval, and weakens when lightweight variants are excluded; see R1–R3.
